explanations.answer: Flee like a bird to your mountain
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. David has just said he takes refuge in the LORD, and then he asks, “How then can you say to me: ‘Flee like a bird to your mountain!’” It's like telling a man who's already home to go look for a house. Pack up, fly off, find a mountain. David isn't taking that advice.

explanations.answer: Hide away in the cave of Adullam
explanations.explanation: A cave is a good guess for a hiding spot, but there's no cave in this psalm. The advice David hears is about a bird and a mountain. Hiding places are easy to mix up. I'd mix up my own oven if you spun me around twice.

explanations.answer: Sail away on a ship to Tarshish
explanations.explanation: There's no ship in this psalm, friend. The advice David hears is “Flee like a bird to your mountain!” (Psalm 11:1). So this escape plan flies, it doesn't sail. Keep the bird in mind and you've got it.

Yes, baker. The wicked set their arrows on the string “to shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart.” They're hiding while they aim, which tells you something about them. David puts it plainly, and I think he wants us to feel how unfair that is.

This psalm doesn't name the poor and needy. The people in the shadows are aiming at the upright in heart. The poor and needy are a good group to care about, but they aren't who the arrows are pointed at here. Look back at verse 2 and the answer is right there.

The widow and the orphan don't show up in this psalm. The wicked bend their bows and shoot from the shadows at the upright in heart. It's easy to grab a familiar group when you're thinking about people who need protecting. Here David names someone else, so keep your eye on that phrase.

That's it. The question goes, “If the foundations are destroyed, what can the righteous do?” A foundation is what everything else sits on. When I'm pressing cookies, if the counter wobbles, nothing else matters. That's why this question lands so hard.

Walls sound like a solid guess, but this psalm never mentions them. The question is about the foundations. Walls are what you build up, and a foundation is what you stand on. That's the word to remember from verse 3.
The temple does show up in this psalm, but later, in verse 4. There it says the LORD is in His holy temple. No gates are mentioned. The destroyed thing in verse 3 is the foundations.

Right, baker. David says, “The LORD is in His holy temple; the LORD is on His heavenly throne.” The advice had a mountain in it, and David's answer starts with where the LORD is. David is looking at the LORD, not at the escape route.

Mount Sinai is a famous mountain, but this psalm doesn't mention it. David is being told to run to a mountain of his own, and he answers by pointing to the LORD in His holy temple. So no mountain is needed. Look at verse 4 again and you'll spot it.

Eden isn't in this psalm. David says the LORD is in His holy temple and on His heavenly throne. The garden is a lovely guess, but this psalm points somewhere else. The answer is in the first line of verse 4.
True, baker. David says, “His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men.” Nothing slips by Him. Even the shadows the wicked hide in are no place to hide from Him.

It's actually true. David says, “His eyes are watching closely; they examine the sons of men.” The LORD is on His heavenly throne, and nothing escapes His eyes. It's an easy one to doubt when the verse sounds so big.
This one is false. David says, “The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked.” Both groups get tested. The word “only” is what trips people up here.

Right, it's false. David says, “The LORD tests the righteous and the wicked.” Both groups, not just one. I'd honestly rather be on the tested list than ignored, because being tested means He's paying attention.
Yes, baker. David says, “His soul hates the lover of violence.” This one is heavy, and I think it hurts to read it slowly. David says it straight, and I'm going to leave it that way.

Money is a good guess when you're thinking about what people love too much, but it's not in this verse. David says the LORD's soul hates the lover of violence. Money isn't mentioned anywhere in the psalm. Look back at verse 5 and the answer is the last words.

Pleasure isn't mentioned in this psalm. In verse 5, David says the LORD's soul hates the lover of violence. A lot of loves could fit in that blank, but the verse names one. Check the second half of verse 5.

That's right, baker. David says, “On the wicked He will rain down fiery coals and sulfur; a scorching wind will be their portion.” This is a heavy verse, so I'll just let it sit. The psalm says it, and David says it plainly.

Hail and great stones aren't in this psalm. In verse 6, David says the LORD will rain down fiery coals and sulfur, with a scorching wind. It does say "rain down," so the guess makes sense. It's a heavy verse, so take your time with it.

Frogs and gnats aren't in this psalm. David says the LORD will rain down fiery coals and sulfur, and a scorching wind will be their portion. This is a heavy verse, so no jokes from me here. Take another look at verse 6.
Yes, baker. David says, “For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice.” Righteous and loving justice go together. It's good news when the One on the throne cares about what's right.
Riches aren't in this verse. David says, “For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice.” Riches sound like something a throne would go with. The psalm names the thing He loves, and it's justice.

Victory isn't the word in this verse. David says, “For the LORD is righteous; He loves justice.” Victory is a fair guess, since the psalm has a lot of tension in it. But the word David uses is justice.
That's right, baker. David ends the psalm with, “The upright will see His face.” After the arrows, the shadows and the heavy verses, this is how it closes. I think that's a good place to land.

Ruling the nations isn't in this psalm. The last line says, “The upright will see His face.” It's easy to expect a crown after all that tension. David closes on something quieter, and I think it's better.
Inheriting the earth isn't in this psalm. David's last line is, “The upright will see His face.” It's a big promise, and the psalm gives a different one. Look at the final sentence of verse 7.
